analogy.p: A satnav that announces “turn left, then you will reach the king’s house” does not drive the car. It tells you where roads lead, and you decide whether to follow. Macbeth treats a partial prediction as an instruction and drives straight to murder. The analogy breaks down because the witches do not simply provide information: they are agents of evil that may also steer Macbeth’s mind.
analogy.t: The witches as a satnav that only says part of the route

bullets: The audience would take the witches seriously as a threat to the king and the state, not as comic pantomime figures.
Daemonologie argued that the devil tempts people and sometimes tells partial truths to lure them, which fits Banquo’s warning about the “instruments of darkness”.
Witches were thought to control the weather; the witches’ storm and the ship tossed at sea (Act 1 Sc 3) echo the North Berwick accusations.
The “sailor’s wife” revenge story (Act 1 Sc 3, early) shows petty spite and the power to harm at a distance.
Witches were often poor, old women; Shakespeare’s witches are unusual because they speak with prophecy and political importance.
The weird sisters get their name from an old word for fate, linking them to destiny as well as to evil.

callouts.p: A 1597 book by James I, written as a dialogue, arguing that witchcraft is real and a serious crime against God and the state.

Say what the belief implies for the audience’s reaction: ‘a Jacobean audience, believing witches could raise storms, would have found the opening thunder and lightning frightening, not just atmospheric.’

core.h: Witchcraft in Jacobean England and Scotland
core.p: In Shakespeare’s time most people believed witches were real, and many thought they were servants of the devil. James I had a personal interest: in 1590 to 1591 he took part in the North Berwick trials, where people were accused of raising storms against the ship carrying him and his new wife home from Denmark. In 1597 he published Daemonologie, a book written as a dialogue about the devil, magic and witches. In 1604 a new Witchcraft Act made invoking evil spirits a crime punishable by death.

bullets: The play opens with the witches, not with Duncan, which signals that the supernatural will frame the human story.
The first scene is very short and introduces key words: “battle”, “fair”, “foul”, “hurly-burly”.
The witches always appear in threes and speak in short phrases, which increases the sense of a chorus rather than individuals.

Their final scene (Act 4 Sc 1) is their longest, with Hecate and a dance; some editors think the Hecate passages were added by another writer, so be cautious about claiming them as Shakespeare’s own art.

callouts.p: When you quote a witch, mention the rhythm: ‘The trochaic tetrameter, in contrast to the iambic pentameter of the human characters, creates a spell-like effect.’

core.p: The witches speak in a different verse form from the other characters. They chant in short rhyming lines with a heavy, falling rhythm (trochaic tetrameter) while noble characters mostly speak in iambic pentameter. The effect is incantatory and unsettling: the witches sound like spells, nursery rhymes turned sinister. Their favourite device is paradox, which signals that their world is upside down.

core.h: The prophecies and how they are fulfilled
core.p: The witches’ first predictions to Macbeth are all true: he is Thane of Glamis already, he becomes Thane of Cawdor within minutes, and he becomes king. The fulfilment of the first two predictions gives the third power, which tempts him towards action. Banquo’s prophecy, to be “lesser” and “greater”, is a paradox that resolves when his descendants become kings while Macbeth dies childless. In Act 4 the apparitions deliver equivocal assurances which turn out to be technically true but cruel.

bullets: Evidence for fate: the witches (weird sisters) know the future; prophecies come true despite Macbeth’s efforts (Fleance escapes but Banquo’s line still reigns).
Evidence for free will: Banquo’s different reaction; Macbeth’s own soliloquy in Act 1 Sc 7 proves he understands the choice; Lady Macbeth’s manipulation is human.
Macbeth is tragic because he is responsible: he knows the moral law yet breaks it.
The Jacobean audience believed in providence: God’s order will be restored, so the usurper’s success must be temporary.
A compromise reading: the witches offer a temptation, but their words only work because of the person who hears them.

callouts.p: ‘Shakespeare leaves ambiguous whether the witches are cause or catalyst, but the weight of evidence suggests…’
Speaking with deliberately ambiguous or double meaning, so that a statement is technically true but misleading.

core.p: One of the central debates is whether Macbeth is destined to fall or chooses it. The text supports both readings. Macbeth’s aside “If chance will have me king” suggests he could wait, but he immediately thinks of murder; Banquo hears the same prophecy and does not act. A grade 9 response explains that the witches’ words become dangerous only because they meet Macbeth’s ambition and his wife’s urging.

bullets: Lady Macbeth’s invocation (Act 1 Sc 5): she calls on spirits to “unsex” her; a deliberately sinful act that parallels witch-like summoning.
The dagger (Act 2 Sc 1): the hallucination appears just before the murder and then seems to be covered with blood, mirroring his imagination.
Banquo’s ghost (Act 3 Sc 4): only Macbeth sees it, which suggests guilt or a supernatural visitation; the banquet scene shows his public self falling apart.
The apparitions (Act 4 Sc 1): staged as a ritual, they show the witches’ hold at its strongest.
The sleepwalking scene (Act 5 Sc 1): not supernatural, but the psychological counterpart of the ghost, showing guilt that no spirit is needed to cause.

callouts.p: The supernatural moves from external (witches) to internal (guilt), which shows the consequence of choice.

core.p: The witches are not the only supernatural presence. Other moments are ambiguous: they might be spirits, or they might be Macbeth’s guilt. Shakespeare gives the audience both options, which builds dramatic tension and complicates responsibility.

bullets: Opening scene with witches sets the tone before any human character speaks.
First meeting (Act 1 Sc 3) is the inciting incident for Macbeth’s ambition.
Banquo’s doubt gives a contrasting voice that the audience can trust.
The second meeting (Act 4 Sc 1) is the midpoint of Macbeth’s moral decline; he has become the seeker.
The final collapse of the prophecies in Act 5 gives the tragedy its catharsis.

callouts.p: Say that the supernatural gives hamartia a tempter: it shapes the tragic structure without removing responsibility.

core.p: The supernatural does several jobs. It creates atmosphere and suspense; it drives the plot by supplying prophecy; it expresses theme (appearance and reality, fate and free will); and it gives the audience the pleasure of dramatic irony when they see how the prophecies can be misread. Structurally, the witches’ meetings bookend Macbeth’s climb and fall: he meets them as a hero in Act 1, seeks them out as a tyrant in Act 4, and discovers their deception in Act 5.

bullets: Start with a thesis that takes a view on the witches’ power.
Use at least one structural comment: how the supernatural develops across the play.
Always analyse a word, not just a line.
Bring in Banquo as a foil.
Use tentative verbs: “suggests”, “could imply”, “perhaps”.
End by evaluating Shakespeare’s purpose: to explore responsibility, to reflect Jacobean fears, or to create tragic irony.

callouts.p: Some editors believe these were added by another writer. Safer to build your analysis on the witches’ speeches in Act 1 and Act 4 Scene 1 apart from Hecate.
callouts.t: Do not over-claim the Hecate scenes

core.h: Exam technique: writing about the supernatural
core.p: Most questions on the supernatural will be framed as theme, character or ideas. Do not describe scenes; select two or three moments and show how language and structure create an effect. Use alternative interpretations to show a high-level argument, and fold in the context of witchcraft naturally.

plan: The witches’ first appearance: inversion and unnatural bodies (Act 1 Sc 1 and 3), Daemonologie context
Prophecy and choice: Macbeth’s aside versus Banquo’s warning
From outside to inside: Lady Macbeth’s invocation, the dagger and the ghost
Act 4: the apparitions as equivocation, the cauldron scene as spectacle
Resolution: “the equivocation of the fiend” and responsibility
essays.q: Explore how Shakespeare presents the supernatural in Macbeth.
essays.text:
Shakespeare presents the supernatural as a force that tempts but never compels. From the moment the witches chant “Fair is foul, and foul is fair”, the audience senses a world where moral categories can be reversed. The rhyming trochaic rhythm, so different from the iambic verse of the human characters, makes the witches sound like a spell, while the chiasmus of “fair” and “foul” reflects the inversion that Macbeth will bring to Scotland. For a Jacobean audience familiar with James I’s Daemonologie and with the 1604 law against witchcraft, these figures would have seemed genuinely dangerous agents of the devil.

Yet the more we examine their influence, the more it seems to depend on Macbeth. Banquo notices that the witches’ “beards forbid me to interpret” their sex, so their bodies are unnatural, and he warns that the “instruments of darkness” tell small truths to ruin us. Macbeth, by contrast, starts at their words. Banquo asks why he seems to “fear things that do sound so fair”, a question that suggests the fear is of his own thoughts. Macbeth’s aside, “If chance will have me king”, shows that he considers leaving it to fate, but his mind has already drifted to murder. The witches say what will happen, never what he must do, so Shakespeare places responsibility with the human choice.

As the play progresses, supernatural moments become increasingly private. Lady Macbeth invokes spirits in Act 1 Scene 5 using imperatives such as “Come”, which reverses the usual order: she commands the dark, as a witch might, and a Jacobean audience would recognise this as a sinful act. In Act 2 Scene 1 the dagger is ambiguous; Macbeth himself asks whether it is a vision “proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain”, and the broken rhythm of the soliloquy suggests a mind dividing. By Act 3 Scene 4 the ghost is visible only to him, so the supernatural has become an expression of guilt. A modern reader may see these as psychological, whereas a Jacobean audience could take them as real spirits; Shakespeare leaves both readings available.

The cauldron scene in Act 4 returns us to the witches, but now they respond to Macbeth’s demand. “Something wicked this way comes” is spoken by a witch, so Macbeth is the intruder in a world he once feared. The three apparitions give prophecies that are technically true: Macduff was “untimely ripp’d”, and Birnam Wood moves as camouflage. Macbeth’s overconfidence is a tragic flaw, not a result of magic; he hears what he wants to hear.

By Act 5 he recognises “the equivocation of the fiend / That lies like truth”. The word “equivocation” links to the Porter and to the real fear of double speech after the Gunpowder Plot, and it makes the witches sound like conspirators. Even so, one could argue that Macbeth is blaming the fiend for a path he chose. Shakespeare ends with the supernatural exposed as ambiguous, forcing the audience to weigh fate against free will.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare uses the supernatural not to excuse Macbeth but to externalise his ambition: the witches offer equivocal possibilities, and every supernatural moment after them becomes more internal until the “fiend” is revealed as a mirror of Macbeth’s own choices.
why: AO1: sustained argument that the supernatural moves from external temptation to internal conscience, rather than listing scenes.
AO2: close attention to rhythm (trochaic against iambic), chiasmus, imperatives, rhetorical question and the word “equivocation”.
AO3: Daemonologie, the 1604 Act and the Gunpowder Plot context are used to explain how the audience would respond.
Alternative interpretations: real spirits versus psychological projection; the witches as cause versus catalyst.
Structured development shows the play’s shape (Act 1 to Act 5) without narrating plot.

mistakes.r: Argue they tempt and equivocate; the decision to murder is Macbeth’s, shown by Banquo’s different reaction.
mistakes.w: Saying the witches make Macbeth kill Duncan.

mistakes.r: Discuss their effects: paradox, trochaic chant, unnatural bodies; explain Jacobean belief that they were real threats.
Select two or three, analyse language, and link to a theme such as ambition or appearance and reality.
Focus on Act 1 and Act 4 Sc 1 witch speeches; if you mention Hecate, flag the editors’ uncertainty.
mistakes.w: Quoting Hecate lines as definitely Shakespeare’s.

mistakes.r: Explain the effect: belief in real danger makes the opening scene frightening for the audience.
mistakes.w: Context as a list: “James wrote Daemonologie, so he liked witches.”

mistakes.r: Use Banquo’s warnings as a foil to show alternative responses to temptation.
Offer both readings: supernatural versus guilt; say which is more convincing and why.
mistakes.w: Claiming the dagger and ghost are definitely real (or definitely imagined).

quotes.a: The witches’ chant sets the play’s governing paradox. Balanced antithesis and the chiasmus of “fair” and “foul” make morality seem reversible, so good and evil swap places. The rhyming trochaic rhythm gives it the feel of a spell. It foreshadows Macbeth, who will call himself noble while murdering, and the audience learns at once that appearances cannot be trusted.
quotes.c: Inversion in a Jacobean world where witches threaten order.
quotes.q: Fair is foul, and foul is fair

quotes.a: Macbeth’s first line echoes the witches’ paradox before he has met them. This either shows he is already linked to the supernatural, or that evil is in the air itself. The mixture of foul weather and fair victory fits his own mixed state as a hero about to become a traitor. The echo is a structural device, linking him to the witches.
quotes.c: Contemporary belief that witches could affect the weather.
quotes.q: So foul and fair a day I have not seen
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 3, Macbeth’s first words, early in the scene

quotes.a: Banquo notices the witches’ beards, so he cannot tell their gender. Their androgyny blurs a boundary Jacobeans took as fixed, making them unnatural and unsettling. Banquo’s rational attempt to “interpret” contrasts with Macbeth’s eager acceptance. His scepticism makes him a foil for the hero.
quotes.c: Great Chain of Being; gender roles as part of natural order.
quotes.q: your beards forbid me to interpret
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 3, Banquo confronting the witches

quotes.a: Banquo warns that evil forces tell small truths to lure us to destruction. “Instruments” makes the witches tools of a greater power, and “darkness” belongs to the play’s light and dark imagery. His analysis is accurate and prophetic, yet Macbeth ignores it. Dramatic irony: the audience hears the correct reading of the temptation.
quotes.c: Daemonologie: James thought the devil used witches to tempt.
quotes.ref: Act 1 Sc 3, Banquo’s warning to Macbeth
quotes.t: metaphor, light and dark imagery, foreshadowing

quotes.a: Macbeth briefly trusts fate: if destiny wants him king, it can crown him without his help. The conditional shows the real choice. He turns immediately to thoughts of murder, which suggests the witches did not make him evil, only awakened what was there. A reader could say fate and ambition are in tension throughout.
quotes.c: Renaissance debate on free will and predestination.
quotes.q: If chance will have me king
quotes.t: aside, conditional clause, tension between fate and free will

quotes.a: Lady Macbeth, alone, invokes spirits to “unsex” her and fill her with cruelty. The imperative verbs show she commands, not begs, the supernatural; she chooses to become evil. Her speech is placed straight after reading Macbeth’s letter, so the human tempter takes over from the witches. A Jacobean audience would see it as a witch-like act of summoning.
quotes.c: Witchcraft Act 1604 criminalised invoking evil spirits.

quotes.a: The rhetorical question shows Macbeth uncertain if the dagger is real. Shakespeare leaves open whether it is supernatural, guilt, or imagination. The dagger leads him (“marshal’st me the way”) towards the king’s room, a sign that his own mind has now become the tempter. The soliloquy’s broken rhythm mirrors his anxiety.
quotes.c: Jacobeans might have thought it a devil’s illusion.
quotes.q: Is this a dagger which I see before me
quotes.ref: Act 2 Sc 1, Macbeth’s soliloquy before the murder
quotes.t: rhetorical question, hallucination, soliloquy, hallucination vs supernatural

quotes.a: The chant’s repeated sounds and strong rhythm create a hypnotic spell. “Toil and trouble” suggests the work of evil and the disorder it causes. The ingredients that follow, often from foreign or outcast things, appeal to Jacobean fears of the unclean and the alien. The ritual sets the stage for the apparitions.
quotes.c: Contemporary ideas of witches’ potions and cauldrons.
quotes.ref: Act 4 Sc 1, opening and refrain of the cauldron scene

quotes.a: The witch senses Macbeth’s approach and calls him “wicked”. The witches now label him as one of their own. The simple, rhythmic line has an ominous sing-song tone, and Macbeth’s arrival makes him seem the intruder in their world. It shows how far he has fallen since he was “Bellona’s bridegroom”.
quotes.ref: Act 4 Sc 1, the Second Witch, early in the scene

quotes.a: Macbeth finally calls the witches’ prophecies a double-talking trick. “Fiend” identifies them with the devil, and “equivocation” links to the Porter and to Jacobean fears of ambiguous speech. The delayed realisation is tragic irony: he believed the half-truths he wanted. It can also read as him blaming the witches for his own choices.
quotes.c: Equivocation and the Gunpowder Plot trials.
quotes.ref: Act 5 Sc 5, Macbeth realises he has been tricked

summary: Understand Jacobean belief in witchcraft (James I’s Daemonologie, the North Berwick trials and the 1604 Witchcraft Act), how Shakespeare presents the witches, prophecies and other supernatural moments, and the debate between fate and free will.

terms.d: Deliberately ambiguous speech that is technically true but misleading.
A statement that seems contradictory but contains a deeper truth.
A verse rhythm of four stressed-unstressed beats per line, used for the witches’ chants.
A verse line of ten syllables in five unstressed-stressed pairs, the usual rhythm of noble speech.
A character who contrasts with another to highlight qualities; Banquo is a foil to Macbeth.
The tragic flaw or error that leads to a protagonist’s fall.
A ghostly appearance; in Act 4 they are the three prophetic visions.
When the audience knows something a character does not.
A speech where a character speaks thoughts aloud alone on stage.
